notes.b: Survival swimming is different from swimming for speed or fitness. Its aim is simply to keep you alive after something goes wrong in the water.
points: The purpose is to stay alive and reach safety after an unexpected fall into water.
The swimmer is often clothed and cold, so the skills must conserve energy and heat until rescue arrives, because a tired, chilled swimmer cannot keep going for long.
notes.tip: Survival swimming appears as a named activity in written answers, so be ready to link it to safety and to conserving energy.

notes.b: How you enter the water matters most when you do not know what is in it. The safest entry depends on whether the depth and the hazards are known.
points: When conditions are unknown, enter feet first and slowly, sliding in, so your feet meet any hidden obstacle or shallow bottom before your head does.
A straddle entry (jumping in with one leg forward and one back) is used in known deep water, and it keeps the head above the water so you can see and breathe.

notes.b: Sometimes a survival swimmer has to go under the surface, for example to pass beneath a hazard or reach an object. A surface dive is a controlled way of going from swimming at the top of the water down to depth.
points: Submerging feet first: push down with the arms, with the legs together, so the body sinks vertically.
Head-first surface dive: bend at the hips, then drive the legs up vertically, so that the weight of the legs above the water pushes the body down.
Feet-first surface dive: rise slightly, then sweep the arms up so the body sinks vertically feet first.
The feet-first surface dive is useful in unknown water, because your feet lead and meet any hidden hazard or shallow bottom before your head does.

notes.b: Floating lets you rest and save energy while you wait for help. It works because a relaxed body with the lungs filled with air stays at the surface.
points: Lie back with the head back and the ears in the water, which helps the body lie flat and stay up.
Spread the body and limbs to increase surface area, so the weight is supported over a larger area of water.
Breathe calmly while floating, so you keep your energy and stay relaxed.
Floating works with or without a buoyancy aid (equipment that helps you stay afloat, such as a lifejacket).

notes.b: Treading water keeps your head above the surface while you stay in one place. It relies on the legs and hands working together, and the hands use a movement called sculling.
points: Treading water: keep the body upright.
Treading water: the legs use an eggbeater kick (the legs rotate alternately in circles) or a breaststroke-type kick (the legs push out and round, then squeeze together).
Treading water: the hands scull flat, moving back and forth near the surface.
Sculling: figure-of-eight hand movements push water down to keep the head up or to move gently.

notes.b: Most people who fall in are fully dressed, and clothes change how you swim. You need a plan for staying afloat and moving without wasting energy.
points: Clothes trap water and add drag (resistance that slows you down), so swimming is harder and tires you faster.
Use slow, efficient strokes: breaststroke, sidestroke or back strokes with the arms under water, so you save energy over a long time.
Keep clothing on in cold water, where it provides insulation (it helps keep body heat in).
Maintain good form throughout, so the strokes stay efficient even as you tire.

notes.b: Underwater swimming means travelling beneath the surface for a short distance. It has one safety rule that must never be broken.
points: Use a breaststroke-type arm and leg action.
Keep the eyes open, so you can see where you are going.
Underwater swimming is used to escape surface hazards.
Never hyperventilate (take a series of deep, fast breaths) beforehand, because it suppresses the urge to breathe and can lead to blackout underwater.
notes.tip: Never recommend hyperventilating before underwater swimming.

notes.b: Survival swimming includes swimming a longer distance, so you also need to turn efficiently at the end of a length.
points: Efficient open turns (turns made at the wall without a tumble) are made at the wall.
Efficient turns help keep a steady pace over the distance, so you do not lose rhythm or waste energy.

notes.b: Cold water takes heat from the body quickly. HELP is a position that cuts heat loss for a swimmer who is on their own.
points: HELP stands for Heat Escape Lessening Posture.
The swimmer floats with a buoyancy aid (equipment that helps you stay afloat) and draws the knees up to the chest.
The arms are crossed over the chest.
HELP protects the main areas of heat loss: the head, armpits and groin.
notes.tip: In cold water the HELP and HUDDLE positions keep you still, which is why they conserve heat.

notes.b: HUDDLE is the group version of HELP. Staying close together shares heat.
points: HUDDLE is performed with at least two others, each wearing a buoyancy aid (equipment that helps you stay afloat).
The group holds each other closely, with chests together, to share heat and stay together.
Children are placed in the middle of the group.
notes.tip: Survival swimming appears in written answers on roles in a group, so know how a group arranges itself in HUDDLE.

notes.h: Cold water shock, hypothermia and keeping still
notes.b: Cold water is dangerous in two ways: a sudden shock on entry, and a slower loss of body heat. Staying calm and still is the main defence against both.
points: On entry to cold water, the swimmer gasps and breathes rapidly. This is called cold water shock.
For the first minute, stay still and calm, and float rather than thrash.
HELP and HUDDLE keep the swimmer still, which conserves heat.
Swimming hard in cold water loses heat faster than keeping still.
Hypothermia is a dangerous fall in body temperature caused by heat loss.
The risk of hypothermia increases with time in cold water, so limit movement to conserve heat, unless safety is very close.
notes.tip: In cold water, swimming hard loses heat faster, so say that staying still in HELP or HUDDLE is the better choice.

keyTerms.definition: Swimming skills used to stay alive and reach safety after an unexpected fall into water, often while clothed and cold.
A flotation device worn to keep the swimmer afloat.
A dive in which the swimmer rises slightly and then sweeps the arms up so the body sinks vertically feet first.
A dive in which the swimmer bends at the hips and drives the legs up vertically so their weight pushes the body down.
Staying on the surface by lying back with the body and limbs spread to increase surface area.
Staying upright in the water with the legs kicking and the hands sculling near the surface.
Figure-of-eight hand movements that push water down to support the body.
The sudden gasp and rapid breathing that occur on entry to cold water.
A dangerous fall in body temperature caused by heat loss, which increases the longer a swimmer stays in cold water.
Heat Escape Lessening Posture, in which the swimmer floats with knees drawn up and arms crossed over the chest to limit heat loss.
A group position in which at least three people, each with a buoyancy aid, hold each other closely to share heat.

questions.prompt: Explain the HELP and HUDDLE positions and why each conserves heat.
questions.model: HELP (Heat Escape Lessening Posture): the swimmer floats with a buoyancy aid, draws the knees up to the chest and crosses the arms over the chest. This protects the head, armpits and groin, which are the main areas of heat loss, and reduces the body surface exposed to cold water. HUDDLE: at least two others, each with a buoyancy aid, hold each other closely with their chests together, so the group shares heat. Children are placed in the middle of the group. Both positions conserve heat by keeping the body still and reducing the exposed surface.

questions.prompt: Describe how to tread water and float to conserve energy.
questions.model: To tread water, keep the body upright, use an eggbeater or breaststroke-type kick for the legs, and scull the hands flat back and forth near the surface, which keeps the head up with little effort. To float, lie back with the head back and the ears in the water, spread the body and limbs to increase surface area, and breathe calmly. Floating works with or without a buoyancy aid. Both skills conserve energy, because the body rests on the water instead of working continuously to stay up.
